works.title: Portrait of a Man Wearing an Ivy Wreath
works.display_title: Portrait of a Man Wearing an Ivy Wreath
works.maker_note: Maker unrecorded. The AIC record gives a culture (artist_title 'Ancient Egyptian') and a region (artist_display 'Egyptian; The Fayum, Egypt'), not a named painter. The AIC's 2025 catalogue entry (Ashley F. Arico, cat. 110) also does not name the painter, and says the sitter's identity is unknown too ('As is true for most panel portraits, the identities of these two men are not known').
works.date: Roman Period, early to mid–2nd century
works.medium: Lime (linden) wood, beeswax, pigments, gold, textile, and natural resin
works.provenance_text: Emily Crane Chadbourne (1871- 1964), Paris, London, and Chicago; given to the Art Institute of Chicago, 1922.
works.provenance_note: The AIC API provenance_text and the 2025 catalogue entry (cat. 110, https://doi.org/10.53269/9780865593213/107) agree word for word: the chain starts with Emily Crane Chadbourne (1871–1964) and ends with her 1922 gift. Neither source gives a findspot, an excavation, a dealer, an acquisition date or an export record, so the panel's history before Chadbourne is unknown. The API gives the place as 'The Fayum, Egypt' (place_of_origin 'Al Fayyum'). The 2025 catalogue says only 'Probably the Fayum, Egypt', and notes that 'Fayum portrait' is an outdated name because such portraits were made all over Egypt. The two sources also give different titles: the API title is 'Portrait of a Man Wearing an Ivy Wreath', while the 2025 catalogue calls it 'Portrait of a Man Wearing a Wreath'. The catalogue explains why: Knudsen and Sabino (2016) and Verri et al. read the wreath as ivy leaves and berries, but Corcoran (2021) suggests convolvulus (bindweed). This record keeps the API title, as R5 requires. The 2016 AIC Roman Art catalogue entry (cats. 155–156) was not consulted because publications.artic.edu returned a Cloudflare 403 to a single fetch on 2026-10-09, and it was not retried.

works.museum_alt_text: A portrait of a young man with dark hair and beard painted on an irregular piece of wood. The background is gold as a wreath of ivy and necklace he wears. There are many areas where the paint has come off the surface.
works.alt: A thin, upright wooden panel with an uneven, angled top edge, shown against a plain grey background. On it is a head-and-shoulders portrait of a young man facing forward. He has large brown eyes, thick dark eyebrows, dark curly hair, a short dark beard and a moustache. A thin gold band with small gold leaves circles his hair. Patches of gold leaf fill the space on either side of his neck and shoulders, and a few small gold squares sit along the neckline of his pale garment. Reddish-brown streaks run down the face and chest, wood grain shows through the worn paint, and dark brown and black patches cover much of the lower third of the panel.

The 2025 catalogue entry is © 2025 The Art Institute of Chicago under CC BY-NC 4.0 (licence line on the entry page, 2026-10-09), so paraphrase and link it only.
works.sensitivities: Funerary portrait of a real, now unnamed person. The 2025 AIC catalogue (https://doi.org/10.53269/9780865593213/107) says panels like this were laid over the face of a mummified person and held in place with strips of linen. It says this panel was trimmed at the top to fit the mummified body it was once attached to, and that resin and mummy wrappings still stick to the surface; the API medium lists 'textile, and natural resin'. The panel is not itself human remains, but it carries burial wrapping material, and the body it belonged to is not recorded in any AIC source (couldn't determine where it is). The catalogue says that 'the vast majority' of such portraits were removed from the mummified people they belonged to because of their modern popularity as art objects. Whether and when this panel was cut from its mummy is not recorded. Sacred use: the catalogue describes these portraits as part of funerary ritual, playing a role in the dead person's transfiguration after death, and links gilded wreaths to Book of the Dead Spells 19–20. Colonial-era removal: the findspot, excavation, export date and route are all unrecorded, and the provenance begins only with Chadbourne, who gave the panel in 1922. Restitution: no claim on this object was found (two web searches, 2026-10-09). Handle as a burial object: no novelty or 'spooky mummy' framing, and do not give the sitter a name or invent a biography.

works.museum_alt_text: An ink and color handscroll of a landscape scene, mountains in the background, a river in the foreground and trees throughout the midground
works.alt: A horizontal section of a silk handscroll, painted in blue-green and dark ink on golden-brown silk. Blue-green mountains run along the top. At left, flat stepped fields stretch back toward the hills, with thin leafless pinkish trees and blue rocks in the foreground. Right of centre, a two-storey pavilion with a railed balcony stands among dark pines. At the bottom, a man stands at one end of a long, narrow boat on open water. On the bank above him are a small figure in red and a standing figure. At lower right, a figure in a dark robe faces a group of robed figures beneath tall pines and pale pink flowering trees.

works.museum_context_paraphrase: Paraphrased from the AIC description field (CC BY 4.0, Art Institute of Chicago), not copied. The scroll illustrates a fable by Tao Qian (365–427) and reads from right to left. A fisherman stumbles on a peaceful farming valley hidden inside a mountain cave. Its people fled political turmoil six centuries earlier and know nothing of what has happened since. Blossoming peach trees, which AIC says symbolise immortality, hide the entrance. AIC links the azurite-blue and malachite-green mineral palette to the 'blue-and-green' manner of which Qiu Ying was a master, and judges from the soft, restrained brushwork that a close follower of his painted it.

The 2009 'Beyond Golden Clouds' exhibition page gives the same: 'Restricted Gift of The Rice Foundation, 1989.625a-b'. The number points to a 1989 accession, but that is inferred from AIC's numbering pattern and is not stated in the record. Who owned the screens before then, and when and how they left Japan, could not be determined.

works.museum_alt_text: A work made of pair of six-panel screens; ink, colors, and gold on paper.
works.alt: Two six-panel folding screens shown side by side, each on a dull gold ground inside a narrow, patterned, pale blue-green border. A dense field of millet fills the lower half of both screens from edge to edge, with long leaves curling over in every direction. The leaves on the left screen are mostly gold-brown, and those on the right screen are mostly olive green. At the top, where the two screens meet, each has a wide dark blue band with a scalloped, cloud-shaped lower edge. A grey disc sits at the top edge of the band on the left screen, and a pale cream disc sits at the top edge of the band on the right screen.

The AIC description says viewers seated on tatami mats would have been surrounded by them, which suggests a room setting. It also says the sun-and-moon pairing on screens carries Buddhist, Daoist and Shinto associations, but it does not describe these screens as ritual or temple objects. The AIC sources do not indicate a colonial-era removal. Two web searches on 2026-10-09 found no restitution claim; they surfaced only AIC pages and unrelated dealer listings. The artwork page says the screens are currently off view.

The AIC's own Handbook of the Department of Oriental Art (Art Institute of Chicago; I could not determine its year from the bookseller listing I consulted, https://www.aseq.it/arte-orientale/31725-handbook-of-the-department-of-oriental-art.html) says the Near Eastern collection 'was given its first impulse by Dr. Frank W. works.museum_alt_text: White ceramic cup with red and blue flowers and square handle.
works.alt: A tall white cylindrical tankard photographed from one side against a plain grey background. On the right is a squared-off handle made of flat straight strips, outlined in blue and painted with blue wavy lines. works.sensitivities: Secular object: a drinking vessel (AIC classification 'drinking vessel'), which the AIC description says may also have served as a flower vase. It is not funerary and not human remains, and no sacred or ritual use is stated in any AIC source (inscriptions null). The provenance is thin: provenance_text is null, and the tankard reached the AIC by about 1913 in trustee Frank W. Gunsaulus's gift. How and when it left Turkey is unrecorded, so I could not determine whether its export followed the rules of the time. As far as the sources show, this is not a colonial-era removal from a colonised territory; it would have left the Ottoman Empire before 1913. Turkey does actively pursue Ottoman-era Iznik ceramics: per AFP (Turkish Minute, 2026-03-20) it is seeking the return of 'dozens of İznik tiles held by France's Louvre Museum' and recovered two 16th-century Iznik tiles from Britain in March 2026. Those claims concern architectural tiles. I found no claim on this tankard or against the AIC (two web searches, 2026-10-09). The object is currently off view (AIC is_on_view false).

works.title: Suzani (large hanging or cover)
works.maker_note: Maker unrecorded. The AIC record has artist_title null, and artist_display gives only a place ('Uzbekistan, probably Tashkent'), not a person. The AIC description (CC BY 4.0, paraphrased here) says suzanis were embroidered by urban Uzbek and Tajik women, often young women making them for their dowry. A designer called a kalamkash drew the pattern on the joined cloth, which was then separated so that each embroiderer could work her own length. It says this hanging is made of four lengths and shows different embroiderers' hands, most visibly in the central blossom, where details are black on one half and lighter brown on the other. No one is named. The same description places such suzanis in eastern Uzbekistan, 'particularly near the oasis cities of Bukhara and Kokand', and the record does not reconcile this with the 'probably Tashkent' attribution.

works.museum_alt_text: A work made of cotton, plain weave; embroidered with silk; pieced.
works.alt: A tall rectangular embroidered cloth photographed flat on a grey background. Rows of large rounded red blossoms almost cover its golden-tan cotton ground. Each blossom is edged with a green leafy stem and sits above a small pale-green disc on a dark stalk. A broad outer band, two blossoms deep, frames an inner rectangle. At the centre of the inner rectangle, a thin eight-pointed star outline holds a ring of eight blossoms around a scalloped red rosette with thin striped rays, and a faint vertical line runs through the rosette. Smaller motifs fill the gaps, among them black-and-cream zigzag-striped pods and small red, cream and pale-blue flowers and leaves. A narrow border of small red flowers on a vine runs around the edge, finished with a dark red binding.

works.sensitivities: Not human remains. The AIC record states no funerary or sacred use. The AIC description (CC BY 4.0, paraphrased) presents suzanis as domestic hangings and covers that young women embroidered for their dowry. Wikipedia's 'Suzani (textile)' adds, without a museum source, that brides presented them to the groom on the wedding day, which is a family and ceremonial use, not a religious one. Colonial era: the AIC date range 1840/1890 straddles the Russian Empire's capture and annexation of Tashkent in June 1865 after the siege of Tashkent (Wikipedia, 'Siege of Tashkent'). Whether this piece was made before or after 1865 couldn't be determined. Provenance gap: the AIC provenance_text begins only with Norman L. Rice in Chicago 'about 1930', so how, when and from whom it left Central Asia is unrecorded, and no export permit is recorded. Attribution: the AIC description says the embroiderers were women and names none, so credit 'makers unrecorded' rather than implying the anonymity was chosen. Restitution: no claim on this suzani was found (2 WebSearch calls, 2026-10-09; the second call ran several sub-queries internally). It is on view now in the AIC exhibition 'Embroidered Traditions from Morocco to Afghanistan' (May 2, 2026–Jan. 25, 2027, per AIC exhibition_history).

works.alt: A long, narrow woven cloth photographed flat on a grey ground, about four times as wide as it is tall, in dark red, golden yellow, dark blue and beige. Two large dark-red ships sit side by side. Each long hull is dotted with white and carries a row of yellow heart shapes. At both ends of each hull, tall prow and stern forms rise steeply outward, edged with stepped stripes of red, yellow and dark blue. On each yellow deck, a dark-blue standing figure is at either end. Inside them are yellow shapes on short legs, each under a red parasol shape, and at the centre are two dark-blue blocks dotted with white under a tall striped frame. works.sensitivities: Ceremonial textile with funerary associations; it is not human remains. The AIC description (CC BY 4.0, paraphrased here) gives the context. Palepai belonged to the Paminggir aristocracy and marked status, perhaps descent. Owning one went with titles, a claim to leadership and other privileges. They were used at rites of passage, including marriage, death and accession to rank, and the red ships are read as the ancestors' upper world, reached by the ship of death. AIC showed this cloth in 'On Loss and Absence: Textiles of Mourning and Survival', Sept. 6, 2025 to Mar. 15, 2026 (API exhibition_history). Whether it is held as sacred or restricted today couldn't be determined: no AIC source states any viewing restriction, and no community statement was found. No findspot is recorded, so the record does not say whether it came from a burial or funeral setting. Its provenance starts with E.M. Bakwin, Chicago, by 2002. Nothing explains how a 19th-century aristocratic heirloom left Lampung. In that period Lampung was under Dutch colonial control (Wikipedia 'Lampung', fetched 2026-10-09, says the Dutch annexed it in 1752; that is a tertiary source and the date was not checked against primary sources). No export record appears in the AIC sources. No restitution or repatriation claim on this palepai, or on Lampung ship cloths in general, was found. One web search on 2026-10-09 returned only museum and dealer listings, and finding nothing does not prove that no claim exists.

works.provenance_text: Probably private collection, Belgium [this and the following according to letter from A. Moraga, Apr. 9, 1985; copy in curatorial object file]; sold to Andrés Moraga, Berkeley, CA, by Apr. 9, 1985 [incoming receipt May 11, 1987]; sold to the Art Institute of Chicago, 1987.
works.provenance_note: The AIC provenance rests on one source: a letter from the dealer Andrés Moraga (Berkeley, CA) dated April 9, 1985, held as a copy in the AIC curatorial file and not public. That letter says the skirt was 'probably' in a private collection in Belgium. The Belgian owner is not named. Neither the API nor the artwork page records when, where, from whom or how the skirt was acquired in the Congo, when it left the Congo, or when it reached Belgium, and neither cites an export permit. Moraga had it by April 9, 1985; the AIC incoming receipt is dated May 11, 1987; the accession number is 1987.163. That leaves a gap of up to about a century between the date given ('19th century'; the page says 'Made 1801–1900') and the first documented owner (1985). Belgium was the colonial power in the Congo, first as Leopold II's Congo Free State from 1885 and then as the Belgian Congo until independence in 1960. That is general history, not stated in the AIC record. So a colonial-era removal is plausible but not documented either way.

works.alt: A long raffia overskirt laid flat on a pale grey ground, more than twice as wide as it is tall. The large central field is deep red-brown, covered in rows of lighter rust L-shapes and chevrons set on the diagonal, with small dark rectangles and dots between them. A beige border runs along the top, the bottom and the rounded right end, with dark brown hooked lines winding through it; at the right end the border changes to a denser pattern of interlocking squares. Near the middle of the top border, a small square of dark and ochre triangles breaks the pattern. works.sensitivities: Funerary context, general to the type and not documented for this object. According to the Palmer Museum of Art's 'African Brilliance' catalogue 36 (https://exhibitions.psu.edu/s/african-brilliance/page/catalogue-36), decorated Kuba raffia textiles are given by family and clan at funerals, shown while the body lies in state, and then wrapped around or buried with the body, or kept by the family. The AIC chose this overskirt for 'On Loss and Absence: Textiles of Mourning and Survival' (Sept. 6, 2025–Mar. 15, 2026) and illustrated it as fig. 2 in the catalogue introduction (API exhibition_history and publication_history). What that catalogue says about it: couldn't determine (not read; the AIC exhibition page returned 403 to the fetch tool). Whether this skirt was ever worn at a funeral, buried or exhumed: couldn't determine. It is not human remains and contains none, per the medium line (raffia and embroidery only). Sacred or restricted use for this specific object: couldn't determine; no AIC source mentions any. Colonial era: it is dated 19th century, and its first recorded owner is a 'probably' Belgian private collection named only in a 1985 dealer letter. There is no record of acquisition or export from the Congo, which was under Belgian rule from 1885 to 1960 (general history). Restitution: no claim on this object was found (two web searches, 2026-10-09). Belgium's 2021 plan with the DRC covers federal (state-owned) collections, not privately held or already exported objects (The Art Newspaper, 2021-12-24, https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2021/12/24/belgium-plans-to-hand-back-colonial-loot-to-dr-congo), so it doesn't reach this skirt. No AIC statement on the object's restitution status was found. Suggest the room text names the provenance gap plainly rather than presenting the skirt as cleanly sourced.

works.provenance_note: The AIC provenance_text begins with Shelly and Kenny Zegart, Louisville, KY, 'by Sept. 7, 2001' (incoming receipt RX23406), and ends with the gift to the Art Institute in 2001 (fiscal_year 2002). The provenance_text does not name the donor; the credit line names Shelly Zegart alone ('Gift of Shelly Zegart'). No owner before the Zegarts is recorded, so where the quilt was between about 1820 and its arrival with them is unrecorded. The AIC publication_history lists Cathy Gaines Florence, Collecting Quilts: Investing in America's Heritage (American Quilter's Society, 1985), and a 2025 New York Times obituary of Shelly Zegart. I have not seen the 1985 book, so I could not determine what it says about the quilt or who owned it then. The AIC exhibition_history lists 'Exploring Quilts: Art, History and Craftsmanship' (2004) and 'Fabric of a New Nation: American Needlework and Textiles, 1776-1840' (2011-2012), both in the museum's textile galleries. Folkstreams says Shelly Zegart co-founded the Kentucky Quilt Project in 1981, which it calls the nation's first statewide quilt-documentation project (https://folkstreams.net/filmmakers/zegart-shelly, read 2026-10-09).

works.museum_alt_text: A work made of cotton, plain weaves; printed; pieced; backed with cotton, plain weave; cotton batting; quilted with cotton thread.
works.alt: A rectangular quilt with rounded corners, laid flat on a black background. Six square blocks sit in two columns of three. Each block holds a large round sunburst: wedge-shaped pieces of tan print and blue-flowered print radiate from a small eight-pointed star of tan print at the centre. Four blocks have a background of small blue-and-tan print. The upper-right and lower-left blocks have a dark blue print scattered with small white leaf shapes. Dark red strips divide the rows, and a dark red zigzag runs down each side border.
looking_prompts: Find the two blocks set on the dark blue print. Where do they sit in relation to each other?

works.sensitivities: A domestic bedcover (AIC term_titles include 'needlework - quilt' and 'bedcover'). The AIC sources record no funerary use, no human remains and no sacred use. Place of origin is Kentucky, and every recorded owner is in Louisville, KY, or Chicago, so no cross-border or colonial-era removal is recorded. The recorded owners are the collectors Shelly and Kenny Zegart; the 2001 gift is credited to Shelly Zegart. No owner before them is recorded. No restitution or ownership claim on this quilt was found (two web searches, 2026-10-09). The maker is unrecorded, and the AIC sources say nothing about who made it or in what circumstances. That could not be determined, and the page should not supply a maker or a story.
